body:
## What belongs in a Newcastle office fitout design brief?

A useful office fitout brief explains what the business needs the workplace to do, what is known about the premises and which decisions are still open. It gives the appointed designer and quoting teams a common starting point. A collection of attractive reference images cannot do that job on its own.

For a Newcastle business, the brief should connect the people using the office with the available building, delivery constraints and business-case budget. Start with the work, then test the layout and specification against it.

Your Office Space provides client-side project management. We help coordinate the agreed brief, budget, scope, programme and client decisions. YOS does not carry out fitout construction as principal contractor. Appointed contractors, designers, certifiers and other specialist advisers retain their respective responsibilities.

[BUTTON: Plan my Newcastle fitout brief]

**Free working pack:** [Download the two-page design brief checklist (PDF)](/guides/office-fitout-design-brief-newcastle-checklist.pdf) or [use the editable text version](/guides/office-fitout-design-brief-newcastle-checklist.txt). No email is required. Use the worksheet to record evidence, owners and the decisions needed from your team.

## Start with a one-page business brief

Describe why the project is happening. Is the business moving, growing, consolidating teams or changing how it works? Write down the problems the current workplace creates and the outcomes that would make the project worthwhile.

Use observable requirements where you can: the number of people present at busy times, the meetings that happen together, visitor arrivals, equipment in use and the storage that must be retained. Separate current evidence from a growth assumption that the business has not yet approved.

Nominate one person to consolidate stakeholder feedback. Staff, IT, finance, operations and leadership can all contribute, but the designer needs an agreed client position and an identified person who can make decisions.

## Describe activities before drawing rooms

| Brief item | Useful information to provide | Question for the appointed team |
| --- | --- | --- |
| People and attendance | Roles, peak attendance and planned changes | Which work settings support the actual pattern? |
| Meetings and privacy | Group sizes, frequency, calls and confidential work | Which spaces need a separate acoustic or privacy response? |
| Visitors and access | Arrival pattern, reception and known access needs | What needs assessment in the proposed layout? |
| Equipment and storage | Dimensions, quantities and operational requirements | What space and service interfaces need investigation? |
| Shared facilities | Existing amenities and building arrangements | What is available, suitable and included in the scope? |
| Furniture | Items to retain, condition and measured sizes | What can be reused within the proposed layout? |

A headcount is useful, but it does not define a whole workplace. An office with frequent client meetings can need a different mix of spaces from a team of the same size doing mainly individual work. Use the [office size calculator](/resources/office-size-calculator) as a planning starting point, then have the layout assessed for the actual brief.

## Gather premises evidence and name the unknowns

Collect the available measured plans, landlord fitout requirements and existing services information. Record who supplied each document and its revision. If a dimension, capacity or condition is unverified, mark it as a question rather than silently using it as a design fact.

The [Newcastle fitout readiness checklist](/blog/office-fitout-readiness-newcastle) helps organise those premises questions. This design brief then explains the outcome you want within that premises, rather than repeating the readiness assessment.

[SafeWork NSW's structures guidance](https://www.safework.nsw.gov.au/hazards-a-z/buildings-and-structures) describes distinct design and construction responsibilities. Share relevant site and operational information with the appropriately appointed team. A business brief does not replace specialist design or a safety assessment.

## Ask the test fit to answer business questions

A test fit can help explore whether a proposed arrangement meets the brief. Ask what information and assumptions support it, which matters still need investigation and what level of design detail it represents. A concept layout is not automatically a construction-ready or approved design.

For example, a hypothetical Newcastle professional-services team might initially request more meeting rooms. A review of its working pattern could instead reveal a need for a mix of small call spaces and one larger shared room. That is a question to test with the designer and users, not a standard answer for every office.

Compare options against the same requirements. Record the trade-offs in usable space, privacy, service implications, furniture reuse and cost information available at that stage. Ask the relevant advisers to assess accessibility, services and approvals for the actual proposal.

[BUTTON: Discuss my workplace design brief]

## Set a whole-project budget before selecting finishes

Tell the team whether the budget includes construction, furniture, services investigations or upgrades, consultant fees, approvals, IT, moves and contingency. State whether figures include GST. Show costs that are quoted separately from estimates and unpriced questions.

The [Newcastle fitout cost guide](/blog/commercial-fitout-cost-newcastle-2026) and [fitout estimator](/resources/fitout-estimator) support early planning. They do not replace site-specific design and quotes. A square-metre rate can hide very different furniture and mechanical scopes, so use it as a guide while the brief and business case develop together.

Separate must-haves from preferences and later-stage options. If an option does not fit the business case, ask what can change in the scope or specification and what consequences follow. Keep specialist performance requirements with the appointed advisers rather than removing them to chase a headline price.

## Agree decision points and control the brief revision

Use a short decision register: question, options, adviser, decision-maker, due date and recorded outcome. Ask the designer and contractor which client decisions are needed before the next stage can proceed.

Keep the brief, drawings, furniture schedule and pricing documents aligned by revision. If the brief changes after quotes arrive, identify what needs repricing. Otherwise two proposals may appear comparable while responding to different instructions.

Before requesting construction prices, confirm with your appointed team what is sufficiently developed for that purpose and what remains an allowance or assumption. Use the [construction quote comparison guide](/blog/compare-office-construction-quotes-newcastle) for the next decision, and the [variations guide](/blog/office-fitout-variations-newcastle) once the agreed scope begins changing.

## Your office fitout design brief checklist

- Record the business reason for the project and the outcomes sought.
- Identify peak attendance, working patterns and growth assumptions.
- List meetings, privacy, visitors, equipment and storage needs.
- Audit furniture to retain with dimensions and condition.
- Collect available premises records and document revisions.
- Mark unverified services and conditions for specialist advice.
- Separate landlord works from tenant requirements.
- State the whole-project budget and GST basis.
- Distinguish essential requirements, preferences and later options.
- Identify the client decision-maker and stakeholder input process.
- Agree design review points, deliverables and unresolved questions.
- Issue one dated brief revision with the relevant supporting documents.

## Turn the brief into a coordinated Newcastle fitout project

YOS can help organise the business requirements, information gaps and decisions under an agreed client-side project management engagement. We can connect the brief with budget and programme discussions while the appointed designer and contractors perform their respective work.

[Explore our Newcastle office fitout project management service](/office-fitout). If landlord works are part of the deal, prepare the [landlord and tenant works schedule](/blog/landlord-tenant-fitout-works-newcastle) alongside the brief.

Tell us the suburb, project stage, available plans, intended working pattern and target timing. You do not need a finished brief to start a conversation.

## Common questions

### What is an office fitout design brief?

It is a record of the business outcomes, people, activities, premises information, budget assumptions and decisions that the appointed design and delivery teams need to understand. It should identify unknowns and document revisions as well as requirements.

### Should we get fitout quotes before preparing a brief?

Early cost discussions can help, but comparable quotes need an agreed scope and clear assumptions. Ask the appointed team what design information is appropriate for the pricing stage and identify any unresolved allowances.

### Is a test fit the same as an approved construction design?

No. Confirm the purpose, detail and limitations of the test fit with its author. Further design, specialist assessment and approvals may be needed before construction.

### Can YOS help with the fitout brief without being the builder?

Yes. Under an agreed client-side engagement, YOS can help organise business requirements, information, budget assumptions and decisions. The appointed designer, contractors and specialist advisers retain their respective responsibilities.

*General business project-planning information only. Confirm design, approvals, safety, lease and contract requirements with the appropriately appointed advisers for the actual project. Scope, fees, timing and availability are agreed individually.*
